mainTopic: Measuring vows of body parts: how far 'hand' and 'leg' reach, how to price a vowed hand, and רבא's questions about reusing an assessment
overview: The amud opens by ending a list of unclear vows ('my width,' 'my sitting,' 'my thickness,' 'my girth') with תיקו. No answer is given. Next, a ברייתא explains רבי יהודה's way of measuring a vow of 'the weight of my hand': he puts the arm into a barrel of water, then adds donkey meat until the water level matches. רבי יוסי objects that this needs guessing, so the hand should simply be estimated directly. רבי יהודה replies that we do as much as we can to be exact. The גמרא then asks how far 'hand' and 'leg' reach. It explains that vows follow how ordinary people talk, while Torah laws like תפילין, washing in the מקדש, and חליצה each have their own source. רב פפא and רב אשי then argue whether this proves something about the ankle bone. A new משנה teaches that one who vows 'the value of my hand' pays what the hand is worth, a case where נדרים are stricter than ערכין. רבא and אביי debate how to price the hand, ending with a slave whose one hand legally belongs to his first master. The amud closes with a chain of questions from רבא about reusing an assessment of a person's value, and the last one continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Four questions about unclear body-measurement vows
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the law is if someone vows to donate his width, his sitting, his thickness, or his girth.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone says 'my width' is upon me, what is the law? 'My sitting,' what is the law? 'My thickness,' what is the law? 'My girth,' what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is continuing a list of questions about vows that use an unclear body measurement, asking how each one should be measured.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each wording could mean several different things, so we don't know how much the person must donate. For example, 'sitting' might mean his height when seated. The גמרא wants to know how each of these vows is measured.

keyTerms.meaning: What is it? What is the law? (a request for a ruling)

phrases.english: If he vowed 'his width,' what is the law?
'His sitting,' what is the law?
'His thickness,' what is the law?
'His girth,' what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier series of questions about vows of body measurements.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How to measure a vow that uses the wording width, sitting, thickness, or girth.

steps.title: The questions are left unresolved
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes with תיקו: the questions stay open.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand (unresolved).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא admits it has no answer to these four questions and leaves them open.
steps.deeperAnalysis: תיקו means no source settles the question, so the doubt stays in place. The גמרא now moves on to the next part of the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand: the question stays unresolved

steps.whatToRemember: All four vow wordings (width, sitting, thickness, girth) end in תיקו. The גמרא never decides how to measure them.

phrases.english: Let it stand (unresolved).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the questions of step 1 without an answer.

steps.title: רבי יהודה's method: a barrel of water for the hand or leg
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא expands the משנה: for a vow of the weight of a hand or leg, רבי יהודה says to fill a barrel with water and put the hand in up to the elbow, or the leg up to the knee.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'The weight of my hand is upon me,' etc. The רבנן taught: if someone says 'the weight of my hand' or 'the weight of my leg is upon me,' רבי יהודה says he brings a barrel, fills it with water, and puts in his hand up to the elbow, or his leg up to the knee.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה about a vow to donate the weight of one's hand. Then it brings a ברייתא that starts explaining רבי יהודה's way of measuring that weight.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You can't cut off a hand and weigh it, so רבי יהודה needs an indirect method. This step gives only the first half of it: put the limb into a barrel full of water. The next step finishes the method.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The weight of my hand is upon me' (a vow to donate that amount)

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'hand' (יד) means the whole forearm up to the elbow, not just the palm.

phrases.english: 'The weight of my hand is upon me,' etc.
The Rabbis taught: 'The weight of my hand'
and 'the weight of my leg is upon me,'
Rabbi Yehuda says: He brings a barrel
and fills it with water,
and puts in the hand up to the elbow,
or the leg up to the knee.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשְׁקַל יָדִי עָלַי וְכוּ׳. תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: the משנה's case of the weight of a hand.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהודה: measure the limb by putting it into a barrel full of water (up to the elbow or knee).

steps.title: Using donkey meat to match the weight, with a hint from a פסוק
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה finishes his method: weigh donkey meat, sinews, and bones and add them to the barrel until it is full again. A פסוק hints that donkey flesh is like human flesh.
steps.simpleTranslation: He weighs donkey meat, sinews, and bones, and puts them in until the barrel fills. Even though there is no proof for this, there is a hint, as it says: 'whose flesh is the flesh of donkeys.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה completes his method. After the limb is taken out, donkey meat is added until the water returns to the same level, and its weight counts as the weight of the limb.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is that donkey meat, sinews, and bones fill the same space as the human limb and weigh about the same. He admits this is not a real proof, only a זכר לדבר (a hint) from a פסוק comparing people's flesh to donkeys'.

keyTerms.meaning: there is no real proof for the matter
a hint or allusion for the matter (weaker than a proof)

steps.whyThisMatters: The phrase אף על פי שאין ראיה לדבר זכר לדבר appears often in ש״ס. It tells you a פסוק is only a hint, not a real source.

phrases.english: And he weighs donkey meat, sinews, and bones,
and puts them into it until it fills,
phrases.notes: After taking his limb out, he adds the donkey meat until the water climbs back to where it was with his limb inside.

phrases.aramaic: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין רְאָיָה לְדָבָר,
phrases.english: and even though there is no proof for the matter,
there is a hint for the matter, as it is said:
'Whose flesh is the flesh of donkeys.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבי יהודה's measuring method begun in step 3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The weight of donkey meat, sinews, and bones that fills the limb's space counts as the limb's weight.
steps.raayaSupportSource: יחזקאל 23:20, brought only as a hint (זכר לדבר).

steps.title: רבי יוסי: you can't match donkey parts to human parts
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי asks how anyone can get exactly the right amount of meat, sinews, and bones to match the human limb.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי said to him: How is it possible to match flesh against flesh, sinews against sinews, bones against bones?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי attacks רבי יהודה's method, saying it cannot be done accurately.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Flesh, sinew, and bone each weigh differently for the same amount of space. To get the right weight, you would need the exact same mix of each as in the human limb, and nobody knows that mix.

keyTerms.meaning: to match exactly, to line up

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei said to him:

phrases.aramaic: הֵיאַךְ אֶפְשָׁר לְכַוֵּין בָּשָׂר כְּנֶגֶד בְּשַׂר,
phrases.english: How is it possible to match flesh against flesh,
sinews against sinews,
bones against bones?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי יוֹסֵי: הֵיאַךְ אֶפְשָׁר לְכַוֵּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the method described in steps 3–4.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The method only works if the donkey parts are in the same mix as the human limb, which cannot be known.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: we estimate
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה answers that the mix of flesh, sinews, and bones is estimated.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה said to him: We estimate.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה defends his method: we estimate how much of each part to use.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He agrees an exact match is impossible. But a reasonable estimate of the mix is good enough to keep using the barrel method.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda said to him: We estimate.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי יוסי's challenge.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Accepts imprecision and relies on estimation
steps.terutzMaskana: The mix of meat, sinews, and bones is estimated.

steps.title: רבי יוסי: then just estimate the hand itself
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי replies that if we are estimating anyway, we should simply estimate the weight of the hand directly.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי said to him: Rather than estimating, let them estimate the hand.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי pushes back: once you allow guessing, the whole barrel method is pointless.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the final number depends on an estimate anyway, why bother with water and donkey meat? Just estimate the weight of the arm directly. This is רבי יוסי's own view in the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: rather than estimating (that way), since you are estimating anyway

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei said to him:
Since they are estimating, let them estimate the hand.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי יוֹסֵי: עַד שֶׁאוֹמְדִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns רבי יהודה's answer against him.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהודה's answer that we estimate
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If estimation is allowed, the complicated method adds nothing over directly estimating the limb.

steps.title: רבי יהודה's view: we do as much as we can
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains רבי יהודה: we use whatever method gets us as close as possible.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יהודה? We do as much as is possible.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how רבי יהודה would answer רבי יוסי: an estimate inside a careful method is still better than a plain guess.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Estimating only the mix of meat and bone leaves less room for error than guessing the whole arm's weight. So רבי יהודה keeps the barrel method because it gets closer to the truth.

keyTerms.meaning: we do as much as is possible

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יהודה: barrel of water plus donkey meat, with some estimating, because we try to be as exact as possible. רבי יוסי: since we estimate anyway, just estimate the hand directly.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yehuda (how would he answer)?
phrases.notes: This is the גמרא speaking, not רבי יהודה. It asks how he would respond to רבי יוסי.

phrases.english: We do as much as is possible.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives רבי יהודה's reply to רבי יוסי's last challenge.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since estimating is needed anyway, the method seems useless.
steps.terutzMaskana: A partly estimated method is still more accurate than a plain estimate, so we use it.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבי יהודה keeps his method because we do as much as possible to be accurate.

steps.title: Hand up to the elbow, or only up to the wrist?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says a vowed יד goes up to the elbow, but כהנים wash their יד in the מקדש only up to the wrist.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתא said the hand goes into the barrel up to the elbow. But another source teaches that washing hands and feet in the מקדש goes only up to the wrist.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the ברייתא's rule that a vowed 'hand' goes up to the elbow. Then it points out a source that seems to say 'hand' stops at the wrist.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same word, יד, seems to have two different sizes. For the vow it means up to the elbow. For the כהנים' washing in the מקדש it means only up to the wrist. Which one is it?

keyTerms.meaning: And they set them against each other: the גמרא is raising a contradiction between two sources
The washing of hands and feet that כהנים do before Temple service

phrases.english: With the hand, up to the elbow;
And they raised a contradiction:
Washing of hands and feet in the Temple
is up to the wrist.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the measuring method and asks about the size of the 'hand' being measured.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's rule that a vowed יד is measured up to the elbow
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Another source treats יד as ending at the wrist, so the same word seems to mean two different things.

steps.title: Torah language versus everyday language
steps.stepSummary: In the Torah יד means up to the wrist, but vows follow how ordinary people talk, and people call the arm up to the elbow a 'hand.'
steps.simpleTranslation: In the Torah, 'hand' means up to the wrist. But for vows, we go by how people normally speak.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction by saying the two sources use two different kinds of language.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The washing in the מקדש is a Torah law, so it uses the Torah's meaning: up to the wrist. A נדר is something a person says himself, so we read it the way people normally talk. In everyday speech, 'hand' reaches up to the elbow.

keyTerms.meaning: Of the Torah; here, the meaning of a word as the Torah uses it

keyTerms.term: בִּנְדָרִים הַלֵּךְ אַחַר לְשׁוֹן בְּנֵי אָדָם
keyTerms.meaning: With vows, go after the way people speak: a vow is understood by everyday usage

steps.whyThisMatters: The rule that vows follow everyday speech comes up all over the laws of נדרים.

phrases.english: In the Torah's language, up to the wrist;
with vows,
go after the language of people.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא עַד הַפֶּרֶק, בִּנְדָרִים הַלֵּךְ אַחַר לְשׁוֹן בְּנֵי אָדָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing contexts: Torah language versus everyday speech
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We assumed יד has one fixed meaning everywhere.
steps.terutzMaskana: The Torah's יד is up to the wrist. A vow's יד follows everyday speech, which is up to the elbow.

steps.title: But תפילין show the Torah's 'hand' is the upper arm
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the claim that the Torah's יד means up to the wrist, because by תפילין the Torah's 'your hand' means the biceps.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does the Torah's 'hand' really mean up to the wrist? By תפילין it says 'your hand,' and the school of מנשה taught that this means the biceps!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer it just gave. It brings a case where the Torah's word 'hand' clearly means much higher up the arm.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 10 said that in the Torah, יד stops at the wrist. But תפילין are put on the biceps, and the Torah calls that place 'your hand.' So the Torah's יד seems to reach the upper arm, not just the wrist.

keyTerms.meaning: But look: this word opens a counter-proof
תפילין, worn on the arm and the head
The bulge of the biceps on the upper arm

phrases.english: And in the Torah's language, is it up to the wrist?
But regarding תפילין,
where it is written 'your hand,'
and the school of מנשה taught:
'Your hand': this is the biceps!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּדְאוֹרָיְיתָא עַד הַפֶּרֶק? וְהָא גַּבֵּי תְּפִילִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer from step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the Torah's יד means up to the wrist
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: By תפילין the Torah's יד means the biceps, which is much higher than the wrist.

steps.title: Three separate rules for the word 'hand'
steps.stepSummary: In the Torah יד includes the whole arm up to the biceps. Vows follow everyday speech. The wrist rule for washing in the מקדש is a received tradition.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the Torah, 'hand' includes the whole biceps. With vows, we go by how people speak. And washing hands and feet in the מקדש up to the wrist is a law we know by tradition.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes its answer. It now gives each case its own source for how far 'hand' goes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah's basic meaning of יד is now the whole arm up to the biceps, which fits תפילין. Vows still follow everyday speech, which means up to the elbow. The washing in the מקדש stops at the wrist, but not because of the plain meaning of the word. That comes from a special tradition.

keyTerms.meaning: All of it; the entire biceps area
They learned it as a received law: a tradition, not a reading of the word

steps.whatToRemember: יד in the Torah = up to the biceps (תפילין). יד in a vow = up to the elbow (everyday speech). יד for washing in the מקדש = up to the wrist (a tradition).
steps.confusionAlert: The wrist rule for the כהנים' washing is NOT the Torah's plain meaning of יד anymore. It is a special tradition just for that law.

phrases.english: In the Torah's language, the entire biceps;
with vows,
go after the language of people;
and washing of hands and feet in the Temple,
they learned it as a received law.
phrases.notes: Meaning the wrist limit comes from a tradition, not from the word יד itself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the תפילין challenge from step 11 by reworking the answer from step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the Torah meaning and giving the Temple case its own source (a tradition)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The Torah's יד means up to the wrist, as shown by washing in the מקדש.
steps.terutzMaskana: The Torah's יד goes up to the biceps. The wrist limit for washing in the מקדש is a special tradition. Vows follow everyday speech.

steps.title: Leg up to the knee, or only the foot?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא measures a vowed רגל up to the knee, but a source on the festival pilgrimage suggests רגל means only the foot.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתא said the leg goes into the barrel up to the knee. But another source teaches that the word 'רגלים' leaves out people with artificial feet!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on to the next part of the ברייתא, about the leg. It raises a new contradiction, and the answer will come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא treats רגל as reaching up to the knee. But the רגלים source excludes a person who has only a stump instead of a foot. This suggests that 'רגל' means the foot itself, below the ankle.

keyTerms.meaning: Festivals of going up to ירושלים; literally 'legs' or 'feet'
People with artificial feet or stumps instead of feet

phrases.english: With the leg, up to the knee;
And they raised a contradiction:
'Festivals' (literally 'feet'): this excludes people with artificial feet!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the hand to the leg, using the same kind of contradiction as step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's rule that a vowed רגל is measured up to the knee
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Excluding people with artificial feet suggests that רגל means only the foot, not the leg up to the knee.

steps.title: Vows follow everyday speech, so רגל reaches the knee
steps.stepSummary: The Torah's רגל means the foot, but in vows people call the leg up to the knee a 'רגל'.
steps.simpleTranslation: With vows, we follow the way ordinary people talk.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 13. The Torah's רגל means only the foot, but a vow follows how people talk, and people call the leg up to the knee a 'רגל'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer has the same shape as the answer about יד in step 10. The Torah meaning (foot only) and the vow meaning (up to the knee) are two different things, so the ברייתא and the pilgrimage source do not contradict each other.

phrases.aramaic: בִּנְדָרִים הַלֵּךְ אַחַר לְשׁוֹן בְּנֵי אָדָם,
phrases.english: With vows, follow the language of people.

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּנְדָרִים הַלֵּךְ אַחַר לְשׁוֹן בְּנֵי אָדָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 13 using the same split between Torah meaning and everyday speech that was used for יד.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the two contexts: Torah wording versus everyday speech
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The Torah's רגל and the vow's רגל must mean the same thing.
steps.terutzMaskana: The Torah's רגל means the foot. A vowed רגל reaches the knee, because that is how people talk.

steps.title: Challenge from חליצה: the Torah's רגל seems to reach the knee
steps.stepSummary: If the Torah's רגל is only the foot, why is חליצה valid anywhere from the knee down?
steps.simpleTranslation: Does the Torah's רגל really mean only the foot, so that people with artificial legs are excluded? But by חליצה the Torah says 'his foot', and the משנה teaches that if she did חליצה from the knee and below, it is valid!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the claim that the Torah's רגל means only the foot. It brings proof from חליצה, where the Torah says 'his foot' and the shoe may still be removed from anywhere up to the knee.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah uses the word 'רגלו' for חליצה, and the משנה says any spot from the knee down is valid. This suggests the Torah's רגל reaches the knee, which would undercut the answer of step 14.

keyTerms.meaning: Of the Torah, the Torah's usage
The ceremony that frees a widow from יבום, done by removing the brother-in-law's shoe

phrases.english: And in the Torah, does it come to exclude people with artificial legs?
phrases.notes: This points back to the pilgrimage source in step 13, which read רגל as the foot only.

phrases.english: But regarding חליצה, where it is written: 'his foot',
and it was taught: if she did חליצה from the knee and below,
her חליצה is valid!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the first half of the step 14 answer, that the Torah's רגל means only the foot.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the Torah's רגל means only the foot
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: By חליצה the Torah says 'רגלו', yet the halacha allows any spot from the knee down. So the Torah's רגל seems to include the leg up to the knee.

steps.title: חליצה is different because the פסוק says 'from upon his foot'
steps.stepSummary: The extra word 'מֵעַל' adds the area above the foot, which is why חליצה works up to the knee.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is different there, because the פסוק says: 'from upon his foot'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that חליצה is a special case. The פסוק does not just say 'his foot'. It says 'from upon his foot', which adds the area above the foot.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רגל in the Torah still means just the foot. The leg up to the knee is included in חליצה only because of the extra word מֵעַל, 'from upon'. That is an exception for חליצה, not a new meaning of רגל.

phrases.english: It is different there,
since the verse says: 'from upon his foot'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends step 14 against the חליצה challenge.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Special wording in the פסוק makes this an exception
steps.terutzHavaAmina: חליצה shows that the Torah's רגל itself reaches the knee.
steps.terutzMaskana: רגל is the foot. The word מֵעַל adds the area above it for חליצה.

steps.title: Then why not above the knee too?
steps.stepSummary: If 'מֵעַל' adds the area above the foot, why not the area above the knee as well?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, then above the knee should also be valid!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer. If 'from upon' means 'above the foot', then the thigh is also above the foot, so חליצה should work there too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word מֵעַל has no clear stopping point. The challenge asks why it stops at the knee, since the משנה only allowed 'from the knee and below'.

phrases.english: If so, above the knee also?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges how far the answer of step 16 reaches.
steps.kashyaTarget: Reading מֵעַל as 'anything above the foot'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Everything above the knee is also above the foot, so it should be valid. But the משנה limits חליצה to the knee and below.

steps.title: 'From upon' means only one section above, not above-the-above
steps.stepSummary: מֵעַל covers only the section right above the foot (up to the knee), not the section above that.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'From upon' — but not 'from upon what is from upon'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that 'from upon' adds only the one section directly above the foot, which is the lower leg up to the knee. The thigh is above that section, so it does not count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The leg is treated as sections stacked on top of each other. מֵעַל reaches one level up from the foot and stops there. The thigh would be 'above the above', and the פסוק does not include it.

keyTerms.meaning: Above what is above, a second level up

steps.whatToRemember: The Torah's רגל means the foot. חליצה reaches the knee only because מֵעַל adds one section above the foot, and no more.

phrases.english: 'From upon', but not 'from upon that which is from upon'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 17 by limiting מֵעַל to a single section.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting how far the extra word reaches
steps.terutzHavaAmina: מֵעַל includes everything above the foot.
steps.terutzMaskana: מֵעַל includes only the section right above the foot, up to the knee.

steps.title: רב פפא: so the ankle bone must reach the ground
steps.stepSummary: From the 'one section above' rule, רב פפא learns that the ankle bone is part of the foot.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: Learn from this that the ankle bone goes down to the ground. If you think it is a separate section, then the ankle bone would be 'from upon', and the shin would be 'from upon what is from upon'.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא draws a conclusion about the body from the last step. The ankle bone must reach the ground and belong to the foot section. Otherwise the shin would be two levels up, and חליצה on it would be invalid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says חליצה works up to the knee, so the shin must be only one level above the foot. That works only if the ankle is part of the foot itself and not a separate layer in between.

keyTerms.meaning: If it enters your mind, if you think
It is separated, a separate section

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: Learn from this,
this ankle bone goes down to the ground,
for if you think it is separated,
then the ankle bone would be 'from upon',
and the shin would be 'from upon' of 'from upon'.
phrases.notes: That would make חליצה on the shin invalid, which goes against the משנה's 'from the knee and below'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the conclusion of step 18 to learn a fact about the body.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ankle bone reaches the ground and is part of the foot, not a separate section.

steps.title: רב אשי: anything next to the foot counts as the foot
steps.stepSummary: Even if the ankle is a separate piece, it sits right next to the foot, so it counts as part of the foot.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: Even if you say it is separated, anything right next to the foot is treated like the foot.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי rejects רב פפא's proof. Even if the ankle bone is a separate piece, it is right next to the foot, so it counts as the foot. The shin is then only one level up either way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב פפא assumed a separate ankle would form its own layer. רב אשי says something touching the foot belongs to the foot's section. So the חליצה rule does not prove anything about how the ankle is built.
steps.whatToRemember: רב פפא learns from חליצה that the ankle is part of the foot. רב אשי says there is no proof, because whatever is right next to the foot counts as the foot.

phrases.aramaic: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא מִיפְסָק פְּסֵיק,
phrases.english: Rav Ashi said: Even if you say it is separated,
anything that is next to the foot is like the foot.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר אֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא מִיפְסָק פְּסֵיק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference of step 19.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only רב פפא's proof about the ankle bone. The חליצה rule itself stays.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רב פפא assumed a separate ankle bone would count as its own layer. In fact, anything right next to the foot is part of the foot's section.

steps.title: Vowing the value of one's hand
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that one who vows the value of his hand pays the difference between his worth with the hand and without it, which shows that נדרים are stricter than ערכין here.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If someone says 'The value of my hand is upon me,' we figure out how much he is worth with the hand and without the hand. Here vows are stricter than ערכין.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה starts. It says that if someone promises to give the value of his hand to the Temple, the court figures out how much his hand is worth to him, and he pays that amount.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A vow of דמים (market value) works on any part of a person, so the hand has a real price. A vow of ערך (the fixed amount set by the תורה) does not work on a hand, so a person who says 'the ערך of my hand' pays nothing. That is why the משנה calls this a case where נדרים are stricter than ערכין.

keyTerms.meaning: The market value (what something is worth)
Vows (here, vows to give someone's market value)
Fixed values set by the תורה, based on age and gender

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up דמים and ערך. דמים is what a person would sell for on the market. ערך is a fixed amount from the תורה that has nothing to do with his market price.

phrases.english: MISHNA: 'The value of my hand is upon me' —
they appraise him, how much he is worth
with the hand and without a hand.
This is a stringency of vows over valuations.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה. The earlier discussion about the foot and ankle is finished.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone who vows the value of his hand pays the difference between his worth with the hand and without it. A vow of ערך on a hand would bring no payment at all.

steps.title: How do we figure out the value of the hand?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what method the court uses to appraise the hand.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: How do we appraise him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a practical question about the משנה: how exactly do we measure his value 'with a hand and without a hand'? This question sets up the discussion that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה gives the rule but does not say how to do the math. There are different ways to picture a person 'without a hand,' and each one gives a different price.

phrases.english: GEMARA: How do we appraise him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how to carry out the rule of the משנה in step 21.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The method for figuring out how much a person is worth with his hand compared to without it.

steps.title: רבא: use the method of injury damages
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that we appraise the hand the same way a court appraises someone whose hand was cut off in an injury case.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: We estimate him the way we estimate in damage cases.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the question. We use the method from נזקין, where the court compares the victim's value as a slave before the injury to his value after it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In נזקין, the injured person is priced like a slave, once whole and once with the hand cut off. The difference is the payment. רבא says to use the same comparison for this vow.

phrases.english: Rava said:
We estimate him with the estimate of damages.
phrases.notes: In damages, the court pictures the victim as a slave and compares his price with the hand and with the hand cut off.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא אוֹמְדִין אוֹתוֹ אוֹמֶד שֶׁל נִזָּקִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 22.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Compare him whole to him with his hand cut off, the same way as in injury cases.

steps.title: אביי: injury cases are not the same
steps.stepSummary: אביי objects: in damages the man is really maimed and looks worse, but here the man is whole, so the damages method would make him pay too much.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: Are they the same? There, the man is lowered in value. Here, the man is in good shape.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי challenges רבא and says the comparison to injury cases does not fit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In נזקין the person really lost his hand. An amputated man looks damaged, so his price drops more than just the use of the hand is worth. The man making this vow still has his hand, so using the damages drop would make him pay more than he actually promised.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it comparable? (a way of rejecting a comparison)

phrases.english: Abaye said to him: Is it comparable?
There, the man is lowered in value,
phrases.notes: 'There' means the injury case, where the hand was actually cut off.

phrases.english: here, the man is in good condition.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבא's answer in step 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's idea of using the נזקין appraisal for this vow.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In damages the drop includes the 'damaged man' effect of an amputation. This vower is whole, so that extra loss should not be counted.

steps.title: אביי: compare a one-handed worker to a two-handed worker
steps.stepSummary: אביי suggests a different method: how much less would a buyer pay for a slave who works with one hand than for one who works with two.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: We estimate how much a person would want to pay for a slave who works with one hand compared to one who works with two hands.
steps.whatsHappening: After rejecting רבא's method, אביי offers his own way to measure the hand's value.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי wants to price only the work the hand does, not the 'damaged look' of an amputated man. So he compares the price of a slave working with one hand to the price of one working with both hands.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
We estimate how much a person wants to pay
for a slave who does work with one hand
compared to one who works with his two hands.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי אוֹמְדִין כַּמָּה אָדָם רוֹצֶה לִיתֵּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a new answer to step 22, replacing רבא's method that was rejected in step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Price a slave who works with one hand against a slave who works with two hands.

steps.title: A one-handed slave is the same as רבא's case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what 'one hand' means. If the other hand is cut off, this is exactly רבא's method.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is 'his one hand'? That the other one is cut off? That is the same thing!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges אביי's suggestion by asking what kind of slave works with only one hand.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The usual reason a slave works with one hand is that the other hand is cut off. That brings back the amputated, 'damaged man' case that אביי himself rejected. So his method has not really changed anything.

keyTerms.meaning: That is the same as that (no real difference)

phrases.english: 'His one hand,' what is it,
that the other one is cut off?
That is the same as that!
phrases.notes: He means it is the same as רבא's damages method, which אביי just turned down.

steps.triggerLanguage: יָדוֹ אַחַת מַאי נִיהוּ וְאִידַּךְ פְּסִיקָא הַיְינוּ הָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks אביי's method in step 25 using אביי's own objection from step 24.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's idea of a slave 'working with one hand.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A one-handed slave is an amputee, so his price has the same 'damaged man' problem that אביי used against רבא.

steps.title: A slave whose one hand belongs to his first owner
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא changes the case: compare a full slave to a slave whose bill of sale says one hand still belongs to his first master.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, his hand is written over to his first master.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes אביי's method. 'One hand' does not mean the other hand is cut off. It means the second hand is legally owned by the slave's earlier master.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this case the slave's body is whole, so there is no 'damaged man' effect. The buyer simply does not own the work of one hand. The drop in price measures only what the use of that hand is worth, which matches a person who still has his hand.
steps.whatToRemember: The vow of דמי ידי is measured by the drop in price for a slave whose hand is legally kept by someone else, not a slave whose hand is cut off. This way the hand's usefulness is priced without the extra drop for looking damaged.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the vow is priced by what the person actually promised, the use of a hand that still exists, and not by the larger loss of a real injury.

phrases.english: Rather, his hand is written over
phrases.notes: His bill of sale says the rights to one hand stay with someone else.

phrases.english: to his first master.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 26 by changing what 'one hand' means in אביי's method.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case (the hand is legally assigned to someone else, not physically missing).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'One hand' meant the other hand was cut off, which would be the same as רבא's damages method.
steps.terutzMaskana: Compare a full slave to a whole-bodied slave whose one hand is owned by his first master. This prices only the use of the hand.

steps.title: Does an assessment for damages count for a vow of one's value?
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks whether a person already assessed by three judges for נזקין can use that number when he later vows 'דמי עלי', or whether a fresh assessment by ten is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא asked: A court assessed a person the way it does for damages, and then he said, 'My value is upon me.' What is the law? Do we say he was already assessed once, so we use that number? Or is an assessment by ten different from an assessment by three?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא opens a new question. A person was already valued by a court of three for an injury case, and now he vows to give his own value to the בית המקדש. Can the old number be used?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Valuing a person for a vow needs ten (nine judges and a כהן), while valuing for נזקין needs only three. One side says the number is already known, so why repeat it. The other side says ten is a stricter process, so an assessment by three cannot replace it.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked / raised a question that is not yet decided
The way a court assesses a person's value in a damages (injury) case
'My value is upon me': a vow to give one's market value to הקדש
An assessment or estimate of value

steps.whyThisMatters: This question opens a whole chain. Each later question in the chain assumes an answer to this one.

phrases.english: Rava asked:
They assessed him with an assessment for damages,
and then he said, 'My value is upon me.' What is the law?

phrases.aramaic: מִי אָמַר: הָא אֲמָדוּהוּ חֲדָא זִימְנָא,
phrases.english: Do we say: they already assessed him one time,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִילְמָא שָׁאנֵי אוּמְדָּנָא דְּבֵי עַשְׂרָה
phrases.english: or perhaps an assessment by ten is different
phrases.notes: The משנה in סנהדרין says valuing a person for a vow needs ten: nine judges and a כהן.

phrases.english: from an assessment by three?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic. It leaves the discussion of valuing a hand and asks about reusing an earlier assessment.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Can a damages assessment made by three replace the assessment by ten needed for a vow of 'דמי עלי'?

steps.title: Vowing a second time after already being assessed by ten
steps.stepSummary: Assuming an assessment by three does not count, רבא asks about a person who was properly assessed by ten for one 'דמי עלי' and then vowed again. Can the same number be used, or might his value have risen in between?
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say that an assessment by ten is different from one by three, then what about this case: he said 'My value is upon me,' they assessed him, and then he said 'My value is upon me' again. What is the law? Here ten certainly assessed him. Or perhaps his value went up in between?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא builds the next rung of his ladder. He takes the strict answer to the first question and asks about a case where ten really did assess the person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem of 'three versus ten' is now gone, because ten did the assessment. The only remaining worry is time: between the first vow and the second, the person may have become worth more, so the old number may be too low.

keyTerms.meaning: 'If you will say': assume one answer to the earlier question and build a new question on it
And he went back and said again
In between, in the time between the two events

steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not deciding the first question here. 'אם תמצא לומר' only means 'suppose the answer is the strict one'; the first question is still open.

phrases.english: If you will say:

phrases.aramaic: שָׁאנֵי אוּמְדָּנָא דְּבֵי עֲשָׂרָה מֵאוּמְדָּנָא דְּבֵי תְּלָתָא,
phrases.english: an assessment by ten is different from an assessment by three,
then if he said, 'My value is upon me,' and they assessed him,
and he again said, 'My value is upon me,' what is the law?
Here ten certainly assessed him,
or perhaps he went up in value in between?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the strict answer to step 28 and asks the next question in the chain.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: When ten have already assessed him, can that assessment be reused for a second vow, or must we worry that his value rose in the meantime?

steps.title: Two vows before any assessment was made
steps.stepSummary: רבא's third question: the person vowed 'דמי עלי' twice before any assessment took place. Is one assessment enough for both vows? The question continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said 'My value is upon me,' and they did not assess him, and then he said 'My value is upon me' again. What is the law? Here certainly...
steps.whatsHappening: רבא climbs one more rung. Now both vows came before any assessment, so the question is whether a single assessment can cover both.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This question assumes the answer to step 29 was 'yes, we worry he went up in value in between.' Here no assessment came between the vows, so that worry seems weaker. The sentence breaks off at 'הכא ודאי' ('here certainly') and finishes on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: And they did not (yet) assess him
'Here certainly': opens the first side of the question

phrases.english: If he said, 'My value is upon me,' and they did not assess him,
phrases.notes: The גמרא assumes the words 'if you say we worry he went up in between' here, so this question builds on step 29.

phrases.english: and he again said, 'My value is upon me,' what is the law?
Here certainly...

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The third rung of רבא's ladder. It assumes the answer to step 29 was that we worry about a rise in value.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: If both vows came before any assessment, does one assessment cover both, since there was no time gap after an assessment?
